title: Estimating the Payoff to Attending a More Selective College
research_question: Does attending a more selective undergraduate college causally raise students' subsequent labor market earnings, and does any such payoff differ by family background? Relatedly, do other college characteristics, such as net tuition costs, affect later earnings beyond the effect of peer selectivity as measured by average SAT scores?
data_description: The primary data come from the College and Beyond (C&B) Survey, which links institutional records (including SAT scores, GPA, and major) for students entering 34 colleges in 1976 to a 1995-97 follow-up survey on 1995 annual earnings, occupation, education, and demographics, supplemented by College Entrance Examination Board and Higher Education Research Institute files providing high school class rank, parental income, and college-average SAT scores. The analysis sample includes 14,239 full-time, full-year workers from 30 institutions (excluding four historically black colleges). The survey collected each respondent's list of other schools seriously considered and whether they applied to and were accepted by each. Robustness analyses use the National Longitudinal Survey of the High School Class of 1972 (NLS-72), restricted to four-year college entrants with 1985 earnings above $5,000 (N=2,127). The unit of observation is an individual student.
institutional_context: U.S. college admission involves a three-stage process: students choose where to apply, colleges independently decide whom to admit based on observable credentials (SAT, GPA) and less-tangible attributes (essays, recommendations, motivation), and admitted students choose among their offers, often influenced by financial aid. Elite colleges select applicants partly on traits that also predict future earnings, so observed earnings differences across colleges of differing selectivity conflate the effect of college quality with student ability and motivation. The 1976 cohort attended schools spanning a wide range of selectivity (average SAT scores from 1,020 to 1,360) and net tuition levels, with substantial variation in financial aid and expenditures per student across institutions. The setting is informative because admissions outcomes from multiple independent screens (different colleges' decisions on the same applicant) reveal information about otherwise unobserved student attributes that admissions committees observe but researchers do not.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: IV — treatment = attending a more selective college, control = attending a less selective college; instrument = college admission offers

key_variables.time_period: 1976 entry cohort, earnings data from early 1990s

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Attending a more selective college does not significantly increase future earnings compared to attending a less selective one.
